write/predict: A language model only predicts. Given “I fed my”, it gives every token in its vocabulary a probability of coming next.
write/loop: To write, pick one token, add it to the end, and feed the longer text back in. Then predict again, one token at a time. That loop is called generating.
write/decode: Each turn rests on one choice: which token to take. Making it is called decoding, reading the model's numbers back out as words.
pick/scores: Say the model weighs three tokens: cat, dog and fish, with ids zero, one and two, and scores two, one and zero. Softmax gives cat about two thirds.
pick/greedy: The simplest decoding takes the tallest bar, the argmax: cat, every time. It is called greedy because it grabs what looks best right now, with no thought for later.
pick/dull: So greedy text repeats itself. In 2019, Ari Holtzman and colleagues showed that decoding for the most likely words gives text that is bland and strangely repetitive.
pick/sample: The other way is to sample: pick at random, with those probabilities. Lay the bars end to end, so together they span exactly one, and throw a dart. It lands on cat about two times in three.
pick/shannon: That is how Claude Shannon wrote fake English in 1948, in A Mathematical Theory of Communication: each word picked at random, by how often it follows the word before.
pick/book: His dart was a book: open it anywhere, read on to the last word written, and copy the word after it.
temp/dial: Between safe and varied, a temperature, T, sets where to stand: divide every score by T before the softmax.
temp/name: The name comes from physics, where the chance of a state goes as e to the minus its energy, over the temperature: softmax, with the score as minus the energy. Heated, a system spreads over many states. Cooled, it settles into the lowest.
temp/gaps: Dividing matters because softmax only sees the gaps between the scores, and dividing stretches or shrinks every gap.
temp/cold: Cool it to T equals one half, and the scores double: four, two and zero.
temp/cold-p: e to the four, about fifty five, out of a total near sixty three, gives cat zero point eight seven: sharper, closer to greedy.
temp/hot: Heat it to T equals two, and the scores halve. The bars flatten, and cat falls to about a half.
temp/order: Either way, cat stays on top. Dividing by the same positive T keeps the order, so greedy still picks id zero.
limits/freeze: Push T toward zero, and the gaps stretch without limit. Cat takes everything: greedy, again.
limits/karpathy: In 2015, Andrej Karpathy did this to a model that wrote one character at a time, trained on Paul Graham's essays. It wrote “is that they were all the same thing that was a startup”, over and over.
limits/boil: Push T up without limit, and every gap shrinks to nothing. Each token gets a third: uniform, all equally likely, like a fair die.
limits/between: In between, Karpathy found, a lower T writes more cautiously, and a higher one with more variety and more mistakes.
